```{r}
#| label: setup
# Run R/01_prepare.R and R/02_prevalence.R first.
# This report only reads their outputs. It types no numbers by hand.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(knitr)

here::i_am("reports/report.qmd")

prep_log   <- read_csv(here("output", "prep_log.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
prevalence <- read_csv(here("output", "prevalence.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

weighted <- filter(prevalence, method == "weighted (survey design)")
overall  <- filter(weighted, group == "Overall")
men      <- filter(weighted, level == "Men")
women    <- filter(weighted, level == "Women")
by_age   <- filter(weighted, group == "Age group")
unweighted <- filter(prevalence, method == "unweighted (comparison only)")

pct <- function(row) sprintf("%.1f%%", row$percent)
pct_ci <- function(row) {
  sprintf("%.1f%% (95%% CI %.1f to %.1f)", row$percent, row$ci_lower, row$ci_upper)
}
n_fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

## Summary

Among U.S. adults age 18 and older, an estimated **`r pct_ci(overall)`** had hypertension in August 2021–August 2023. The estimate was `r pct(men)` for men and `r pct(women)` for women. By age group, it was `r paste(sprintf("%.1f%% at %s", by_age$percent, by_age$level), collapse = ", ")`. The analysis included `r n_fmt(overall$n)` NHANES participants.

These are descriptive survey estimates. They describe the population; they don't explain why hypertension is more common in some groups.

## Methods

- **Data:** NHANES August 2021–August 2023 public-use files DEMO_L, BPXO_L and BPQ_L, merged on `SEQN`.
- **Population:** adults 18 and older who were examined, had at least one blood-pressure reading, and were not pregnant.
- **Hypertension:** mean systolic ≥ 130 mmHg or mean diastolic ≥ 80 mmHg (from up to three readings), or now taking prescribed blood-pressure medication. People never told they had high blood pressure were not asked about medication; they count as not taking it.
- **Weights and design:** MEC exam weight (`WTMEC2YR`), strata and PSUs, with the design built on all examined participants and then subset. 95% confidence intervals use the Korn–Graubard method.

## Who was included

```{r}
#| label: prep-log
prep_log |>
  filter(n_before != n_after | step == "merge") |>
  mutate(across(c(n_before, n_after), n_fmt)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Step", "n before", "n after", "Reason"))
```

## Prevalence of hypertension

```{r}
#| label: prevalence
weighted |>
  mutate(
    n = n_fmt(n),
    estimate = sprintf("%.1f", percent),
    ci = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", ci_lower, ci_upper)
  ) |>
  select(group, level, n, estimate, ci) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Group", "Level", "n (unweighted)", "Percent (weighted)", "95% CI"))
```

Without survey weights, the overall share would be `r pct(unweighted)`. That figure describes the people examined, not U.S. adults: NHANES samples some groups (such as older adults) more heavily, and the weights correct for it.

## Notes

- Age is top-coded at 80 by CDC, so "80" means 80 or older.
- Source: CDC/NCHS, National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Compare with NCHS Data Brief No. 511 (<https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db511.htm>).
